cues.text: Let us now turn to how the Internet of Things actually works.
In the earlier parts of this session we looked at what IoT is.
Here we open the machine and look at the parts, and at how they talk to one another.
Start with the basic building blocks.
An IoT system consists of physical objects fitted with sensors and actuators, together with connectivity, computation, data platforms and applications.
Think of these as a chain.
At one end is something in the physical world.
At the other end is a person or a business process that makes a decision.
Everything in between exists to carry information along that chain, and sometimes to carry a command back.
Let us take the first two parts: sensors and actuators.
A sensor measures a phenomenon in the physical world.
Typical examples are temperature, vibration, pressure, position or humidity.
A sensor turns something physical, like heat in a motor, into a number a computer can handle.
An actuator does the opposite job.
It changes a physical condition.
Examples are changing the speed of a motor or changing the position of a valve.
So a sensor lets the system sense, and an actuator lets the system act.
Next is the gateway.
A gateway aggregates local devices, translates protocols and forwards selected data.
Picture a factory floor with many small devices, each speaking in its own way.
The gateway collects what they say, translates between their different protocols, and passes on only the data that needs to travel further.
The word selected matters.
Not everything needs to leave the site.
Then we have two places where computation can happen.
Edge processing analyses data near the source, close to the machine itself.
Cloud platforms aggregate information at a larger scale, bringing together data from many devices and many sites.
Now let me describe the diagram that accompanies this section.
Please look at the visual as I walk through it, because the spatial layout matters here.
It starts at the top left with the physical asset.
From the physical asset, an arrow leads to a sensor.
From the sensor, an arrow leads to a local device or gateway.
From that local device or gateway, the flow splits into two paths.
The first path goes to the cloud, where we find history and analytics.
From the cloud, information then flows on to a dashboard and to planning.
This is the slower, wider view, used for understanding trends and making plans.
The second path goes down from the local device to local control.
From local control, an arrow leads to an actuator.
And from the actuator, an arrow leads back to the physical asset.
So this second path forms a loop.
The asset is measured, the local device decides, the actuator acts, and the asset changes.
The diagram shows that the loop closes locally, without needing to pass through the cloud.
Keep that point in mind, because it returns at the end of this chapter.
Now let us look at connectivity, meaning how devices are linked.
Connectivity may use Ethernet, Wi-Fi, cellular, LPWAN or industrial networks.
LPWAN stands for low-power wide-area network, a family of technologies designed for small amounts of data over long distances with little power.
How do we choose among these options?
The source gives five criteria: coverage, reliability, power, latency and data volume.
Coverage is how far the signal must reach.
Reliability is how dependable the link must be.
Power is how much energy the device can afford to spend.
Latency is how long a message takes to arrive.
And data volume is how much data must be moved.
On top of the network sit messaging protocols.
MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol that uses a broker.
In publish/subscribe, a device does not send messages directly to a particular receiver.
It publishes to a named topic, and the broker passes that message on to everyone who has subscribed to that topic.
CoAP supports constrained devices, meaning devices with very limited memory, processing power or energy.
HTTP with REST may suit other applications.
Industrial systems often use protocols such as OPC UA for interoperability, meaning the ability of equipment from different makers to work together.
There is an important warning here.
TCP/IP connectivity alone does not solve incompatible data semantics.
In plain terms, two systems may be able to exchange data perfectly well across a network and still disagree about what the data means.
One system may report a number in one unit and another may expect a different unit.
Being connected is not the same as understanding one another.
Let us make MQTT concrete.
An MQTT sensor publishes to a topic such as factory/line1/motor2/vibration.
Read this from left to right: the factory, then production line one, then motor two, then the vibration reading.
Authorised subscribers receive the events.
The word authorised is important, because not everyone should be allowed to listen.
MQTT also offers three levels of quality of service, called QoS.
QoS 0 is at-most-once delivery.
The message is sent once, and it may be lost.
QoS 1 is at-least-once delivery.
The message will arrive, but it may arrive more than once.
QoS 2 is exactly-once delivery.
The message arrives once and only once.
But notice the qualification in the source.
These guarantees apply to protocol delivery between the participating endpoints.
End-to-end business effects still require idempotency and proper application design.
Idempotency means that doing the same operation twice has the same result as doing it once.
For example, if a duplicate message tells a system to record a reading, the application must be designed so the duplicate does not cause a double effect.
The protocol alone cannot promise that.
Now let us step back and view the whole IoT architecture.
It has four layers.
First, the perception or device layer, where sensors and actuators meet the physical world.
Second, the network or transport layer, which carries the data.
Third, the processing or platform layer, where data is stored and analysed.
And fourth, the application or business layer, where the information is used for real decisions.
Security and governance span all layers.
They are not a fifth layer on top.
They run through every one.
The source also lists essential lifecycle tasks for devices: device identity, provisioning, firmware updates, certificates, health monitoring and retirement.
Device identity means each device can be uniquely recognised.
Provisioning means setting a device up so it can join the system.
Firmware updates keep the device's built-in software current and secure.
Certificates help prove that a device is what it claims to be.
Health monitoring checks that devices are working.
And retirement means taking a device out of service safely at the end of its life.
Finally, let us work through the sizing example, step by step.
Suppose 500 devices each transmit a 120-byte reading every 10 seconds.
First, the event rate.
500 devices, each sending one reading every 10 seconds, gives 500 divided by 10, which is 50 events per second.
Second, the payload rate.
50 events per second, each of 120 bytes, gives 50 times 120, which is 6,000 bytes per second.
Third, the daily total.
There are 86,400 seconds in a day.
Multiplying 6,000 bytes per second by 86,400 gives 518,400,000 bytes, which is 518.4 megabytes, using the decimal convention.
Note the qualification: this figure is before headers, retries and storage overhead.
The real volume would be higher.
What does this teach us?
Edge aggregation can reduce the volume sent over the wide-area network, the WAN.
But we should preserve required high-resolution evidence locally, so that troubleshooting remains possible.
And, returning to the loop in our diagram, an outage-sensitive control loop should not depend on distant cloud round trips.
If a control decision must happen reliably and quickly, it belongs close to the machine.
